With the incoming valid and ready held low nothing moves: that is the idle condition. Also, when the design keeps several items at once - data waiting its turn, the entries of a table, requests in flight - keep them in an array whose depth is a parameter, built the way real hardware builds it: a queue's write and read pointers wrap around, and full and empty are worked out from the pointers or from a count kept beside them; a table or register file has a valid bit for each entry. In the design's own logic, a count of the filled entries is kept in a register that steps up and down as items come and go, or is worked out from the pointers, never by adding up the valid bits of the entries. An item is never dropped or overwritten while it is still needed: when the array is full, the design makes the sender wait. Every entry and pointer gets an initial value, and the idle condition leaves the whole array unchanged. Write invariants about what the entries hold, one for each entry where it matters: which entries are filled, given the pointers, the count or the valid bits, and what a filled entry holds. When entries carry an order or work in flight, add the facts processor engineers write for their buffers: two busy entries are never each older than the other; what was requested minus what came back, added up over the entries, equals the count still outstanding; an entry starts its work only when every older busy entry has finished; the oldest busy entry's address is the address being sent out; and a select that picks one entry has at most one bit set, written as a sum.

Also, when the design keeps several items at once - data waiting its turn, the entries of a table, requests in flight - keep them in an array whose depth is a parameter, built the way real hardware builds it: a queue's write and read pointers wrap around, and full and empty are worked out from the pointers or from a count kept beside them; a table or register file has a valid bit for each entry. In the design's own logic, a count of the filled entries is kept in a register that steps up and down as items come and go, or is worked out from the pointers, never by adding up the valid bits of the entries. An item is never dropped or overwritten while it is still needed: when the array is full, the design makes the sender wait. Every entry and pointer gets an initial value, and the idle condition leaves the whole array unchanged. Write invariants about what the entries hold, one for each entry where it matters: which entries are filled, given the pointers, the count or the valid bits, and what a filled entry holds. When entries carry an order or work in flight, add the facts processor engineers write for their buffers: two busy entries are never each older than the other; what was requested minus what came back, added up over the entries, equals the count still outstanding; an entry starts its work only when every older busy entry has finished; the oldest busy entry's address is the address being sent out; and a select that picks one entry has at most one bit set, written as a sum.

trait: data held in an array: when the design keeps several items at once - data waiting its turn, the entries of a table, requests in flight - keep them in an array whose depth is a parameter, built the way real hardware builds it: a queue's write and read pointers wrap around, and full and empty are worked out from the pointers or from a count kept beside them; a table or register file has a valid bit for each entry. In the design's own logic, a count of the filled entries is kept in a register that steps up and down as items come and go, or is worked out from the pointers, never by adding up the valid bits of the entries. An item is never dropped or overwritten while it is still needed: when the array is full, the design makes the sender wait. Every entry and pointer gets an initial value, and the idle condition leaves the whole array unchanged. Write invariants about what the entries hold, one for each entry where it matters: which entries are filled, given the pointers, the count or the valid bits, and what a filled entry holds. When entries carry an order or work in flight, add the facts processor engineers write for their buffers: two busy entries are never each older than the other; what was requested minus what came back, added up over the entries, equals the count still outstanding; an entry starts its work only when every older busy entry has finished; the oldest busy entry's address is the address being sent out; and a select that picks one entry has at most one bit set, written as a sum.

Also, when the design keeps several items at once - data waiting its turn, the entries of a table, requests in flight - keep them in an array whose depth is a parameter, built the way real hardware builds it: a queue's write and read pointers wrap around, and full and empty are worked out from the pointers or from a count kept beside them; a table or register file has a valid bit for each entry. Every entry and pointer gets an initial value, and the idle condition leaves the whole array unchanged. Write invariants about what the entries hold, one for each entry where it matters: which entries are filled, given the pointers, the count or the valid bits, and what a filled entry holds. When entries carry an order or work in flight, add the facts processor engineers write for their buffers: two busy entries are never each older than the other; what was requested minus what came back, added up over the entries, equals the count still outstanding; an entry starts its work only when every older busy entry has finished; the oldest busy entry's address is the address being sent out; and a select that picks one entry has at most one bit set, written as a sum.

trait: valid/ready handshake and data held in an array: give the main input or the main output a valid/ready handshake with back-pressure: an item moves only on a cycle when valid and ready are both high; as the sender, the design holds valid and its data steady until the item moves; as the receiver, it lowers ready when it cannot take more instead of dropping data. With the incoming valid and ready held low nothing moves: that is the idle condition. Also, when the design keeps several items at once - data waiting its turn, the entries of a table, requests in flight - keep them in an array whose depth is a parameter, built the way real hardware builds it: a queue's write and read pointers wrap around, and full and empty are worked out from the pointers or from a count kept beside them; a table or register file has a valid bit for each entry. In the design's own logic, a count of the filled entries is kept in a register that steps up and down as items come and go, or is worked out from the pointers, never by adding up the valid bits of the entries. An item is never dropped or overwritten while it is still needed: when the array is full, the design makes the sender wait. Every entry and pointer gets an initial value, and the idle condition leaves the whole array unchanged. Write invariants about what the entries hold, one for each entry where it matters: which entries are filled, given the pointers, the count or the valid bits, and what a filled entry holds. When entries carry an order or work in flight, add the facts processor engineers write for their buffers: two busy entries are never each older than the other; what was requested minus what came back, added up over the entries, equals the count still outstanding; an entry starts its work only when every older busy entry has finished; the oldest busy entry's address is the address being sent out; and a select that picks one entry has at most one bit set, written as a sum.
